title: Medical questions
hookLine: modern fiqh on transplants, IVF, end of life, where scholars reason and differ

lines: NONE OF IT NAMED IN THE TEXT.
cards: Brain-dead. A doctor says the word to a family in a hospital corridor late at night, about their father, and gently asks about donating his kidneys. A few floors up, a young couple is talking with a fertility clinic.

At the end of the hall, a grandmother's machines keep her body going after her doctors say they can no longer help. None of this is in the Qur'an by name. The jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba never saw a ventilator.
Yet a Muslim family in that corridor might call a scholar and ask: what does the law say?

teach.h: GOD SENT A CURE WITH EVERY DISEASE.
teach.b: Start with medicine itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Seeking treatment is part of the tradition.
Scholars look for a text that speaks to the new question, reason by analogy from cases that do appear, and weigh the purposes of the law, which we'll meet in two days. That effort is called ijtihad.
Organ transplants: some fiqh councils have allowed donation, within limits, reading it through the verse in surah five that whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of humankind.
Other scholars have objected, out of reverence for the body after death, which the tradition protects.

Fertility: Sunni councils have allowed IVF between a married couple, using their own egg and sperm, and refused a third party's; some Shia authorities have reasoned more widely, allowing some forms of donation.
Same texts, different reasoning, both careful.

teach.h: END OF LIFE: NO KILLING, SOME LETTING GO.
teach.b: End of life: the same verse likens killing one soul to killing all humankind, and scholars read it as forbidding a deliberately ended life.

Some allow stopping treatment that only prolongs dying, when doctors judge there is no hope of recovery, and brain death is still argued. So the answer is often not one fatwa but a few, each showing its reasoning.
That isn't confusion. It's an old method, honestly applied.

how: Muslim patients and families facing questions about transplants, fertility treatment or end-of-life care may ask a trusted scholar or consult the rulings of fiqh councils, which reason from the Qur'an, the hadith and the purposes of the law.

o: a single fatwa every Muslim follows on modern medicine
new medical cases answered by reasoning from old sources
questions the law leaves to doctors, with no say for scholars

p: reasoning to answer a new question
save one life, save all humankind
the married couple's own, no third party
a cure sent down with every disease

s: Islam treats seeking medical treatment as a lack of trust in God
the report in Bukhari says God sent down a cure with every disease.
scholars give a single agreed answer on every medical question
councils and authorities sometimes differ, each showing its reasoning.
the scholars in today's lesson forbid deliberately ending a life
some still allow stopping treatment that only prolongs dying.

games.q: you're a scholar asked about kidney donation after death. there's no verse about kidneys. what's your first move?
o: refuse to answer, since the text is silent.
reason from texts, similar cases and the law's purposes.
games.why: that's ijtihad; fiqh councils reasoned from 5:32 and allowed donation within limits, while others objected out of respect for the body.

practice: Think of one medical decision someone you love has faced, or might, and name it plainly: donation, a treatment, a hard ending.
Ask today's three questions gently: is there a text, is there a case like it, what is the law trying to protect? Then hold the person and the question side by side.
If a hard ending is close for you, or you're thinking of ending your own life, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Medical questions. New cases in medicine, from transplants to fertility to the end of life, that scholars answer by reasoning from the old sources, and on which they sometimes differ. Today's word.
